metadata.title: THE ROLE OF SUBNATIONAL GOVERNMENTS IN ADULT SKILLS SYSTEMS: JAPAN

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD country note does not analyze student microdata from an ILSA (e.g., PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS/PIAAC) and therefore does not define an analytic sample of students, schools, or countries for statistical estimation. The document describes governance structures and allocation of responsibilities for Japan’s adult skills system across national, regional (prefectures), and local (municipalities) levels, including which institutions handle strategy, intelligence, implementation, funding, and delivery. As a result, there are no plausible values (PV) or scaling procedures, and no sampling/replicate weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT, BRR) to apply. If analysts were to extend this work with ILSA microdata, they would need to specify the relevant ILSA cycle, PV handling, and complex survey weights from the microdata documentation; this note itself provides none.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a governance and policy description (a country note) rather than an empirical student-assessment analysis using ILSA microdata. Because there is no cognitive achievement outcome measured with PV-based scaling, plausible values are not applicable. Similarly, there is no missing-data handling described because no statistical model is estimated on an assessment dataset with item nonresponse or missing questionnaire variables.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used a qualitative/policy compilation approach to describe Japan’s adult skills system governance; no student-level analytic sample is constructed or reported.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD country note provides a structured overview of how Japan’s adult skills system is governed across three levels: national (central government), regional (prefectures), and local (municipalities). It summarizes which institutions are responsible for strategy, intelligence, implementation, funding, and delivery across policy areas including VET, HVET, CET, AE, and ALMPs, using tables and an infographic rather than assessment results. The note highlights a predominantly centralized governance model with subnational roles in adapting and implementing national strategies, including local adult education centres and regional employment services. It also describes the institutional stakeholders (e.g., MHLW, MEXT, JEED, NIAD-QE, Hello Work) and their functional responsibilities. No ILSA assessment data, sampling design, scaling, or predictive modeling is conducted, so there are no performance metrics or benchmarks to interpret.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse because the document is not an empirical large-scale assessment study; it is a policy governance country note. Consequently, there is no student sample size, no ILSA cycle/domain, no PV/scaling, and no ML model evaluation. The absence of these fields reflects the document’s descriptive, institutional mapping purpose rather than a reporting gap in an empirical analysis.
